claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets are caused by differences in short-range atomic order.
Identical thermomechanical processing produces a single-phase FCC microstructure in all alloys included in the comparison.
The degree of short-range order influences dislocation-core spreading.
The degree of short-range order influences dislocation slip behavior.
The equiatomic quinary alloy has greater short-range order than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Enhanced short-range order produces local variations in atomic bonding.
Enhanced short-range order produces a more spatially variable potential-energy landscape.
The bonding and potential-energy variations associated with enhanced short-range order impede dislocation motion.
Greater impediment to dislocation motion improves strain hardening.
Greater impediment to dislocation motion alters failure behavior.
Quaternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates than the quinary baseline.
Ternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates than the quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit deformation and failure characteristics different from those of the quinary baseline.
The lower-constituent-count alloys will have measurably less short-range order than the quinary alloy.
Differences in strain hardening and failure behavior will correlate with measured differences in short-range order.
Atom-probe tomography can provide a quantitative measure of short-range order for these alloys.
High-energy X-ray or neutron diffraction can provide a quantitative measure of short-range order for these alloys.
